questions.stem: An object falls to the ground at around 9 metres per second. How long would it take to fall from a plane that was 9 000 metres in the air?
questions.hint: First find how many seconds it takes. Then change seconds into minutes by dividing by 60.

steps.explain: The object falls 9 metres every second. Find how many seconds it takes to fall 9 000 metres.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 144" width="80%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><line x1="30" y1="20" x2="30" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="30" y="14" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >plane</text><text x="30" y="136" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >ground</text><line x1="26" y1="40" x2="34" y2="40" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="60" x2="34" y2="60" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="80" x2="34" y2="80" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="100" x2="34" y2="100" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><line x1="26" y1="120" x2="34" y2="120" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="150" y="40" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 m to fall</text><text x="150" y="62" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9 m every second</text><text x="150" y="86" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >9 000 ÷ 9 = 1 000 seconds</text><text x="150" y="108" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >1 000 ÷ 60 = 16 r 40 → between</text><text x="150" y="124" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >16 and 17 minutes</text></svg>

steps.explain: Change seconds into minutes. There are 60 seconds in one minute.
16 full minutes use up 960 seconds, and there are 40 more seconds.
steps.work:
\(16\times60=960\)   \(1\,000-960=40\)

So the time is 16 minutes and 40 seconds, which is between 16 and 17 minutes.

steps.explain: Check the other options: 26–27 minutes would be 1 560–1 620 seconds, and 9–10 and 6–7 minutes are far too short.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: This tells you how far it falls in one second.
The answer is in minutes, but you will first get seconds.

questions.stem: One can of tomato paste takes up one-tenth of a row in a supermarket shelf. How many cans of tomato paste would be needed to stock (or fill up) three rows on that supermarket shelf?
questions.hint: If one can takes up one-tenth of a row, how many cans fill one whole row? Then find three rows.

questions.stem: Angelena uses a 375 gram packet of fettuccine and one-third of another 375 gram packet. How do you calculate how much fettuccine she used for the meal?
questions.hint: She uses one whole packet. Then she uses a third of ANOTHER packet. How big is that other packet?

steps.explain: She uses one whole packet.
She uses one-third of another packet, and that packet is also 375 g.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 100" width="75%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="10" y="14" width="120" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="70" y="36" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >375 g</text><rect x="140" y="14" width="120" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/><rect x="140" y="14" width="40" height="34" rx="4" fill="#fdba74" stroke="#c2410c" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="160" y="36" font-size="11.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >125 g</text><text x="70" y="66" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >one whole packet</text><text x="200" y="66" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >⅓ of another packet</text><text x="135" y="92" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >375 + 125 = 500 g</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add the two amounts.
steps.work: \(375+125=500\) g, so the calculation is \(375+(\frac13\text{ of }375)=500\).

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: A takes a third of \(750\) (two packets), which is \(250\). B takes a third of \(500\), which is not one of the packets. D multiplies instead of adding.

steps.explain: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: The other packet is also 375 g. Find a third of 375.

keyPoints.text: calculate how much fettuccine she used
keyPoints.note: She used a whole packet plus a part: add them.

questions.stem:
Here are the wage rates for an apprentice that works in shopfitting and kitchen detail joinery. Two sets of wages are shown. Some apprentices are indentured, that is they have a type of permanent contract. The other apprentices are trainees. There are different rates of pay for indentured and trainee apprentices. The pay also changes from first year to the fourth year.

APPRENTICE JOINER

| Year | Indentured | Trainee |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(\$172.60\) | \(\$193.00\) |
| 2 | \(\$234.00\) | \(\$259.50\) |
| 3 | \(\$306.20\) | \(\$336.10\) |
| 4 | \(\$371.90\) | \(\$392.30\) |

Look at the chart of these wage rates.

parts.stem: Where is the error in the chart?

parts.stem: In addition to the weekly rate, these allowances also apply: Industry Allowance \(\$17.40\) per week; Tool Allowance \(\$18.80\) per week. How much would a second year trainee apprentice earn per week, with allowances for tools and for industry?
parts.hint: Start with the second year trainee wage from the table, then add both allowances.

steps.explain: Find the second year trainee wage in the table.
Add the industry allowance and the tool allowance.
Add the allowances to the weekly wage.
Check the other options: \(\$259.50\) leaves out both allowances, \(\$278.30\) adds only one allowance (+\(\$18.80\)), and \(\$297.70\) has an addition mistake.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.note: Use the Trainee column and the row for year 2.

keyPoints.text: allowances for tools and for industry
keyPoints.note: Add both allowances to the weekly rate.

questions.stem:
Look at this sum. Each letter stands for a number. Which number stands for the letter M?

MU × 4 = CU8

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 451 176" width="45%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q17.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="451" height="176"/></svg>

questions.hint: Look at the units digit first: U × 4 ends in 8. Which digit U gives a product ending in 8?

steps.explain: Look at the ones column. U × 4 gives a number that ends in 8.
steps.work: Try the digits: 2 × 4 = 8 ✓ and 7 × 4 = 28 ✓. Every other digit gives a different last digit, so U is 2 or 7.

steps.explain: Now use the fact that U also appears in the tens place of the answer CU8.
steps.work:
If \(U=7\): \(M7\times4\) must be \(C78\), but \(17\times4=68\), \(27\times4=108\), \(37\times4=148\) — the tens digit is never 7. ✗

If \(U=2\): \(M2\times4=C28\). Try \(12\times4=48\), \(22\times4=88\), \(32\times4=128\) ✓

steps.explain: 32 × 4 = 128 reads M U × 4 = C U 8 with M = 3, U = 2 and C = 1.
Check the other options: if M = 1 the number 12 × 4 = 48 is not CU8; if M = 2 then 22 × 4 = 88 is not CU8; if M = 5 then 52 × 4 = 208 does not have 2 in the tens place.
steps.work: The answer is D (M = 3).

keyPoints.text: Each letter stands for a number
keyPoints.note: The same letter is always the same digit. Start with the ones column.

questions.stem: Although we can never know all the prime numbers, what do you think we might be able to say about the sum of two prime numbers? (Hint: a prime number is a number that can only be divided evenly by itself and/or one.)
options: the sum is always an even number
the sum is an even number for all prime numbers except two
the sum is an odd number for all prime numbers except two
the sum is always an odd number
questions.hint: Write down a few prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 … Which of them is even? Try adding some pairs and see whether the sums are odd or even.

steps.explain: List some prime numbers.
steps.work:
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 …

Only 2 is even. All the other primes are odd.

steps.explain: Add pairs of primes and look at the sums.
steps.work:
Two odd primes: 3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 13 = 20, 11 + 19 = 30 → always even.

With the prime 2: 2 + 3 = 5, 2 + 11 = 13 → odd.

questions.stem: Which shape comes next?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 715 396" width="75%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q25.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="715" height="396"/></svg>

questions.hint: Compare the three circles. What is happening to the thickness of the outline and to the size of the circle?

steps.explain: Look at the thickness of the black outline in I, II and III.
steps.work: I has a thin line, II a thicker line and III a very thick line. The outline gets wider each time.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 114" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="4" /><text x="50" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >I</text><circle cx="140" cy="50" r="26" fill="#fff" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="7" /><text x="140" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >II</text><circle cx="230" cy="50" r="22" fill="#fff" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="11" /><text x="230" y="104" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" >III</text></svg>

steps.explain: Look at the size of the circles.
steps.work: The circles get smaller each time: I is the biggest and III is the smallest.

steps.explain: So the next circle (IV) is smaller still and its line is thicker still: almost all black, with only a small white dot in the middle.
steps.work: A small black circle is what comes next.

steps.explain: Find the option that is small and almost completely black.
steps.work: A is a small black circle. B is large. C and D have thin lines. The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Two things change at once: the thickness of the outline and the size of the circle.

questions.stem:
A tiler wants to make a pattern of grey and white triangle tiles. They would look something like this:

How many grey triangles could fit into this space? Start each row with a grey triangle.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 209" width="90%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q26.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="209"/></svg>

questions.hint: Count how many triangles are in one row and how many of them are grey when the colours take turns, starting with grey. Do this for one row, then use all the rows.

steps.explain: Look at the space. It has 3 rows of triangles, and in each row the triangles point up, down, up, down … so the colours take turns: grey, white, grey, white …
steps.work: Every row begins with a grey triangle, as the question says.

steps.explain: Count the triangles in one row. There are 9 triangles that point up and 8 that point down between them, which makes 17 triangles in a row.
steps.work: \(9+8=17\) triangles in each row

steps.explain: Grey is every second triangle, starting with the first one, so the grey triangles are the 1st, 3rd, 5th … 17th.
steps.work: \(1,3,5,\dots,17\) is \(9\) grey triangles in one row

steps.explain: There are 3 rows, and every row starts with grey, so each row has the same number of grey triangles.
steps.work: \(9\times3=27\) grey triangles

steps.explain: Check the other options: 30 would be 10 grey in each row, 25 is not a multiple of 3 and 36 would be 12 in each row.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Start each row with a grey triangle
keyPoints.note: The colours take turns, so find how many triangles are in each row.
Count the grey triangles in one row, then multiply by the number of rows.

questions.stem: How many more grey triangular tiles would be needed if the tiler wanted to continue the parallel pattern that is shown below? (Hint: Do not include the grey tiles that have already been used).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 220" width="90%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t7-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="220"/></svg>

questions.hint: The picture has 4 rows. Find how many grey tiles the whole pattern would have if the grey tiles are placed all through the picture. Then take away the grey tiles that are already shaded.

steps.explain: Look at the picture. It has 4 rows and the same width as the space in Question 26. Using the same pattern (every row starts with a grey triangle, grey and white take turns), each row has 9 grey triangles.
steps.work: \(9\times4=36\) grey tiles for the whole pattern

steps.explain: Count the grey tiles that are already shaded in the picture. They form a stair shape on the left.
steps.work: There are 10 shaded grey tiles: 1 in the top row, 2 in the second row, 3 in the third row and 4 in the bottom row.

steps.explain: Take away the grey tiles that have already been used.
So 26 more grey tiles are needed.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: Do not include the grey tiles that have already been used
keyPoints.note: Find all the grey tiles the pattern needs, then take away the ones that are already shaded.

questions.stem: Anthony works at the AMI Factory as a second year apprentice. He earns around \(\$7\) an hour. He works \(8\frac12\) hours each day from Monday to Thursday plus 4 hours on Friday. Which calculation shows correctly how much he earns each week?
questions.hint: First find how many hours he works in the week. Then multiply by the pay for one hour. Check that the hours really add to the number used in the calculation.

steps.explain: Find the hours from Monday to Thursday.
steps.work: \(4\text{ days}\times8\frac12\text{ hours}=4\times8.5=34\) hours

steps.explain: Add the 4 hours on Friday.
steps.work: \(34+4=38\) hours in the week

steps.explain: Multiply the hours by the pay for one hour.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A multiplies the hours together, which is wrong (and \(7\times4\times8.5\times4\) is not \(258\)). B works out to \(\$238+\$28=\$266\), not \(\$264\), so its answer is wrong. D uses \(37\) hours, but he works \(38\).

steps.explain: Only option C has the right number of hours and the right total.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: \(8\frac12\) hours each day from Monday to Thursday
keyPoints.note: That is 4 days at 8½ hours. Find the total, then add Friday.
Check the hours and the final amount of each option.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

The Plimsoll line is a safety line that is painted on both sides of a ship. A ship may be safely loaded until this line is reached. The circle with the line through it stands for the original Plimsoll Mark. The top line is the deck line. The other symbols (TF, F, TS, S, W, WNA and LR) also have special meanings.

The figures show the amount of water the ship is drawing. This is the amount of water needed for the ship to float. The Plimsoll line is named after Samuel Plimsoll (1824–1898) who was responsible for its introduction.

Look at the chart showing some Plimsoll marks.

parts.stem: From the chart above, what are the numbers for the original Plimsoll Mark and the Deck Line?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 396" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t8-q11.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="396"/></svg>

parts.hint: Find the circle with the line through it (the original Plimsoll Mark) and the top line (the Deck Line). Read the number on the scale next to each.

questions.stem:
Here are some facts:

• A company made 1000 toys.
• They cost \(\$12\) each.
• The company sold them to stores for \(\$16\) each.

How many would the company need to sell in order to cover the cost of the 1000 toys that were made?
questions.hint: First find the total cost of making all 1000 toys. Then find how many toys have to be sold at \(\$16\) to earn that much money.

steps.explain: Find the total cost of making the toys.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 110" width="90%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="340" height="30" rx="4" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#e11d48" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="178" y="28" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >cost to make 1 000 toys: 1 000 × $12 = $12 000</text><rect x="8" y="46" width="340" height="30" rx="4" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="1.8" /><text x="178" y="66" font-size="12.5" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >$16 each → toys needed to earn back $12 000</text><text x="178" y="100" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#4338ca" text-anchor="middle" >12 000 ÷ 16 = 750 toys</text></svg>

steps.explain: Each toy is sold for \(\$16\). Find how many sales are needed to earn \(\$12\,000\).
Check by multiplying: 750 toys at \(\$16\) each.
Check the other options: 250 toys earn only \(\$4\,000\), 500 toys earn \(\$8\,000\) and 1000 toys earn \(\$16\,000\) (more than the cost).
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.text: cover the cost of the 1000 toys
keyPoints.note: Find the total cost first, then how many toys must be sold to get that much money back.

questions.stem: The US dollar is worth about one and two-thirds what an Australian dollar is worth. If I have to pay 75 US dollars, then how would I calculate this in Australian dollars?
questions.hint: One US dollar is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars, so each of the 75 US dollars is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars. Find 1⅔ of 75.

steps.explain: Each US dollar is worth 1⅔ Australian dollars.
steps.work: 1 US dollar \(=1\frac23\) Australian dollars

steps.explain: So 75 US dollars are worth 75 lots of 1⅔ Australian dollars.
steps.work: \(1\frac23\text{ of }75\)

steps.explain: Work it out: 1 of 75 is 75, and ⅔ of 75 is 50.
Check the other options.
steps.work: A takes \(1\frac23\) of \(125\), which is \(208\frac13\), not \(75\). C and D are not the right way to turn US dollars into Australian dollars.

steps.explain: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: One US dollar is worth this many Australian dollars. Multiply 75 by it.

questions.stem: Which set of arrows completes this pattern?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 556" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t8-q25.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="556"/></svg>

questions.hint: The pattern is a 2-by-2 grid. Go round the boxes clockwise, starting at the top left. Count the arrows in each box and see how the number changes.

steps.explain: Count the arrows in each box, going clockwise from the top left.
steps.work:
Top left: 4 arrows (small arrows pointing right).

Top right: 3 arrows (big arrows pointing down-right).

Bottom right: the box with the question mark.

Bottom left: 1 arrow (a white arrow pointing down-left).

steps.explain: The number of arrows goes down by one each time we move to the next box clockwise: 4, 3, … , 1. So the box with the question mark must have 2 arrows.
Look at how the arrows turn. The arrows point right (→), then down-right (↘), then they should point down (↓) or down-left, and finally down-left (↙). Each box turns the arrows clockwise.
steps.work: The missing box has 2 arrows, turned between down-right and down-left.

steps.explain: Find the option with 2 arrows.
steps.work: A has 2 arrows turned the right way. B has 3 arrows, C has 5 and D has 2 arrows pointing the wrong way. ✓ The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Go round the grid clockwise and follow two things: the number of arrows and the way they point.

questions.stem: Look at the shapes below. They are numbered I, II, III, IV, V and VI. Three of these shapes are joined together to make this pattern. Which shapes were used in the pattern? (Hint: the shapes can be rotated.)

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 891" width="85%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t8-q26.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="891"/></svg>

questions.hint: Look at the grey pattern. It has a slanted corner on the left, a flat top and bottom, and a slanted side on the right. Which of the six shapes have a slanted side like this?

steps.explain: Look at the grey pattern. It has two slanted corners on the left (cut at the top and at the bottom), a flat top, a flat bottom, and a long slanted side on the right.
steps.work: Slanted sides: left top, left bottom and right.

steps.explain: Look at the six shapes and find the ones with slanted sides that could make these.
steps.work: IV has one slanted side (its top). V is a trapezium with two slanted sides. VI is a square with straight sides that fills the middle. I is a rectangle, II is a diamond and III is a parallelogram: their sides do not match the sloping corners.

steps.explain: Turn IV, V and VI and fit them together. IV and V give the two slanted corners on the left and the slanted side on the right, and VI fills the gap in the middle.
steps.work: Together they make the grey pattern with no gaps.

steps.explain: The shapes used are IV, V and VI.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.text: Which shapes were used in the pattern
keyPoints.note: Match the sloping sides of the pattern with the sloping sides of the shapes. The shapes may be turned round.

questions.stem: Here is a large and a small shape. How many of the smaller shapes will fit into the larger shape?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 759 297" width="85%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t8-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="759" height="297"/></svg>

questions.hint: Count the cubes in each shape. For the big one, count the cubes on the front face and then think how many cubes deep it is. Then divide.

steps.explain: Count the cubes in the large shape. The front face is 4 cubes wide and 3 cubes high, and the top shows it is only 1 cube deep.
steps.work: \(4\times3=12\) cubes, \(\times1\) deep \(=12\) cubes

steps.explain: Count the cubes in the small shape. The front has 3 cubes: two at the bottom and one on top at the left. The top shows that it is 1 cube deep.
Divide the cubes in the big shape by the cubes in the small shape.
So 4 of the small shapes fit into the large shape.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Count the cubes in each shape and divide the larger number by the smaller.

questions.stem: A children’s book has a total of 28 printed pages plus the front and back covers are also printed. There are illustrations on 22 pages and on the two outside covers (but not the inside covers). On how many pages (including the covers) are there no illustrations?
questions.hint: Count everything that is printed: the 28 pages and the covers. Then find how many of them have pictures. Remember each cover has an outside and an inside.

steps.explain: Find the total number of printed surfaces. There are 28 pages, and each cover has an outside and an inside, so four more surfaces.
steps.work: \(28+2+2=32\) pages in all (28 pages, 2 outside covers and 2 inside covers)

questions.stem:
Which signs (+, −, ×, ÷) can take the place of the symbols ✧, □ and ○ in the sum below? (Each symbol stands for only one sign.)

\(19\;✧\;4\;□\;3\;○\;1=4\;□\;2\)
questions.hint: The right side is 4 □ 2. Think which sign makes a sensible number there. Then try each option on the left side and see which one gives the same answer.

steps.explain: The same sign □ is used on both sides. Work out the right side for each option, then the left side.
steps.work: In every option except A the sign □ is ×, so the right side is \(4\times2=8\). (In A, □ is +, giving \(4+2=6\).)

steps.explain: Work out the left side with the signs in option C: ✧ is −, □ is × and ○ is +.
steps.work:
\(19-4\times3+1\). Do the multiplication first: \(4\times3=12\).

\(19-12+1=7+1=8\)

steps.explain: Compare the two sides.
steps.work: Left side \(=8\) and right side \(4\times2=8\). They are equal ✓

steps.explain: Check the other options.
Only option C makes both sides equal.
steps.work: The answer is C.

keyPoints.text: Each symbol stands for only one sign
keyPoints.note: The same symbol stands for the same sign everywhere, including the □ on the right side.

questions.stem: Which pattern comes next in this series?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 748 448" width="85%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q10.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="748" height="448"/></svg>

questions.hint: Each box has marks in the top row and marks in the bottom row. Count the straight lines and the slanted lines in each row. Do the numbers follow a pattern?

steps.explain: Count the marks in each box. The top row of each box has a bundle of 3 straight lines with a bar through it, then some single straight lines, then slanted lines like “//”. The bottom row has slanted lines like “\\” and then single straight lines.
steps.work:
Box 1: top: 3 bundled + 0 straight + 2 slanted /; bottom: 2 slanted \ + 3 straight.

Box 2: top: 3 bundled + 1 straight + 3 slanted /; bottom: 3 slanted \ + 4 straight.

Box 3: top: 3 bundled + 2 straight + 4 slanted /; bottom: 4 slanted \ + 5 straight.

steps.explain: Find the patterns in the numbers.
steps.work:
Slanted “/” (top): 2, 3, 4 → go up by 1.

Straight lines (top, after the bundle): 0, 1, 2 → go up by 1.

Slanted “\” (bottom): 2, 3, 4 → go up by 1.

Straight lines (bottom): 3, 4, 5 → go up by 1.

steps.explain: Add one more of each to find box 4.
steps.work:
Slanted “/” (top): 5.

Straight lines (top, after the bundle): 3.

Slanted “\” (bottom): 5.

Straight lines (bottom): 6.

steps.explain: Find the option with these numbers.
steps.work: D has the bundle of 3, then 3 straight lines, then 5 slanted “/” on the top row, and 5 slanted “\” and 6 straight lines on the bottom row. ✓ The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Count each kind of line separately in every box and find how each count changes.

questions.stem:
Questions 11 and 12 refer to the following information.

A national survey involving 503 children aged 8 to 13 has found that 44 per cent of girls and 31 per cent of boys expressed concern about their weight, and two-thirds felt they needed more exercise.

It found that children spent more time watching TV or playing computer games than playing sport, although team sport was their favourite activity. On average they watched television for 80 minutes per day; spent 20 minutes playing computer games and on other computer uses, including the Internet; spent 48 minutes playing organised and social sports; and 29 minutes doing homework.

Source: Sydney Morning Herald, 9 April 1997, Australian Horticultural Corporation

The chart shows what kids like doing.

questions.stem:
Six is considered a perfect number. This is because when you add up all the numbers (except 6) that divide into it properly then they add up to six. For instance 1, 2, and 3 all divide properly into six (1 × 2 × 3 = 6; or 2 × 3 = 6).

The next perfect number is 28. What are the numbers (proper divisors) that make 28 a perfect number? (Hint: Do not include 28.)
questions.hint: Find every number that divides exactly into 28 (except 28 itself). Then check that they add up to 28.

steps.explain: Find the numbers that divide into 28 without a remainder. Test the numbers from 1 upwards.
The numbers that divide 28 exactly are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14 (not counting 28).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 84" width="85%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="10" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="38" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >1</text><rect x="76" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="104" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >2</text><rect x="142" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="170" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4</text><rect x="208" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="236" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >7</text><rect x="274" y="8" width="56" height="38" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="302" y="33" font-size="17" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >14</text><text x="180" y="72" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#059669" text-anchor="middle" >1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add them to check that 28 is perfect.
Check the other options: A leaves out 2, B leaves out 1 and C has 5 and 6, which do not divide 28.
steps.work: The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: A divisor divides into the number with nothing left over.

questions.stem:
In a binary number system you only count with zero (0) and one (1). There are no other numbers. Here are our ordinary decimal numbers and the binary number for each one of them.

What would be the binary number for nine (9)?
questions.hint: Each binary digit stands for 8, 4, 2 or 1 (from left to right). Which of these places do you need to add up to 9?

steps.explain: Look at how the table works. Each column of the binary number stands for a number: from the left 8, 4, 2 and 1.
steps.work: A 1 means “use this number”, a 0 means “do not use it”.

steps.explain: Find how to make 9 from 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Put a 1 under 8 and under 1, and a 0 under 4 and 2.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
The answer is D.

keyPoints.note: Each place in a binary number is worth 8, 4, 2 or 1. Add up the places that have a 1.

questions.stem: In this square the numbers (from 4 to 12) add up to 24 across and down. Find the missing number in the square marked with the asterisk (★). (Hint: you may have to find some of the other numbers before you can find the number you want.)

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 451 231" width="45%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q18.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="451" height="231"/></svg>

questions.hint: Every row and column adds up to 24. Find a row or column with only one missing number first.

steps.explain: Look for a row or column with only one missing number. The first row is 9, 5, 10.
Use the left column: 9 + 11 + 4.
steps.work: \(9+11+4=24\) ✓ (so the left column is complete)

steps.explain: Use the top row of the middle column: the middle column has 5, ?, ? and the right column has 10, ?, ★. The numbers 4 to 12 are each used once, so the numbers 6, 7, 8 and 12 are the ones that are left.
steps.work: The numbers used so far are \(9, 5, 10, 11, 4\); the unused numbers are \(6, 7, 8, 12\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 148 148" width="45%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9</text><rect x="52" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5</text><rect x="96" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >10</text><rect x="8" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >11</text><rect x="52" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="96" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="8" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4</text><rect x="52" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" ></text><rect x="96" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#e11d48" text-anchor="middle" >?</text></svg>

steps.explain: Find the middle number. The middle row is 11 + ? + ? = 24, so the two numbers add to 13. The only two unused numbers that add to 13 are 6 and 7.
steps.work: \(6+7=13\) ✓ so the middle row is \(11, 7, 6\) (the middle column needs 5 + 7 + 12 = 24, so the middle is 7).

steps.explain: The bottom row is 4 + ? + ★ = 24.
steps.work: The middle column is \(5+7+?=24\), so the bottom middle is \(24-12=12\). Then \(4+12+★=24\), so \(★=8\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 148 148" width="45%" height="auto" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >9</text><rect x="52" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >5</text><rect x="96" y="8" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="37" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >10</text><rect x="8" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >11</text><rect x="52" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >7</text><rect x="96" y="52" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="118" y="81" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >6</text><rect x="8" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="30" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >4</text><rect x="52" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" /><text x="74" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >12</text><rect x="96" y="96" width="44" height="44" rx="0" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2" /><text x="118" y="125" font-size="19" font-weight="800" fill="#1e293b" text-anchor="middle" >8</text></svg>

steps.explain: Check the right column: 10 + 6 + 8 = 24 ✓. The missing number is 8.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.text: add up to 24 across and down
keyPoints.note: Every row and column adds to 24. Start with a line that has only one missing number.

questions.stem: Which shape comes next?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 715 452" width="80%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q25.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="715" height="452"/></svg>

questions.hint: Each picture has two lines of arrows (a top line and a bottom line). Follow the arrows in the top line and then the arrows in the bottom line. Do they turn the same way?

steps.explain: Look at the two arrows in the top line of each picture, from picture to picture.
steps.work: The arrows in the first line of each shape turn clockwise (the same way as the hands of a clock).

steps.explain: Look at the two arrows in the bottom line of each picture, from picture to picture.
steps.work: The arrows in the second line turn counter-clockwise (the other way round).

steps.explain: The pattern carries on from one square to the next, so use both turning rules once more to get the next picture.
steps.work: Top line: one more clockwise turn. Bottom line: one more counter-clockwise turn.

steps.explain: Find the option that matches.
steps.work: A has the top arrows and the bottom arrows in the positions given by these two turning rules. ✓ The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Follow the top line of arrows and the bottom line of arrows separately: they turn in opposite directions.

questions.stem: What triangular shape would you form if you travelled directly from Sydney to Adelaide then from Adelaide directly to Melbourne and then back to Sydney?
options: a triangle with three sides of different length
a triangle with three sides of equal length
a triangle with a right angle
a triangle with two sides of equal length
questions.hint: Picture the three cities on a map of south-east Australia. Compare the three straight-line distances: are any two the same?

steps.explain: The three straight lines are Sydney to Adelaide, Adelaide to Melbourne and Melbourne to Sydney.
steps.work: Look at them on a map: they are three different journeys.

steps.explain: Compare their lengths. Sydney to Adelaide is the longest. Melbourne is close to both Adelaide and Sydney, but the two distances to Melbourne are not the same as each other.
steps.work: The three sides are all different in length.

steps.explain: Check the other options.
steps.work: Equal sides would need two cities to be the same distance from a third. The angles are not square, so there is no right angle.

steps.explain: The triangle has three sides of different length.
steps.work: The answer is A.

keyPoints.note: Picture the three cities on a map and compare the three straight lines.

questions.stem:
Look at this clock. It is evening in Sydney. The time in Sydney is about 15 hours ahead of the time in the United States.

What would the time be in the United States?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 143 143" width="25%" height="auto"><image href="/oc/t9-q27.jpg" x="0" y="0" width="143" height="143"/></svg>

questions.hint: First read the time on the clock. It is evening, so it is pm. Then go back 15 hours.

steps.explain: Read the clock. The hour hand is near 5 and the minute hand is on 12, so the time is 5 o’clock. It is evening, so it is 5 pm.
steps.work: 5 pm in Sydney

steps.explain: The United States is 15 hours BEHIND Sydney, so take 15 hours away. Go back to midnight first: from 5 pm back to 12 midnight at the start of the day.
steps.work: 5 pm is \(17\) hours after midnight, so \(17-15=2\) hours after midnight.

steps.explain: 2 hours after midnight is 2 am, on the same day (Sydney’s date).
steps.work: 5 pm − 15 hours = 2 am, the same day.

steps.explain: Check the other options: the next day would be going forward, and 1 am or 3 am would be 16 or 14 hours earlier.
steps.work: The answer is B.

keyPoints.note: Sydney is ahead, so the United States is earlier: take away 15 hours.

questions.stem:
These scientific terms or names are arranged in a special series. Which term comes next in the series?

Acid  Electron  Joule  Pressure  ?
questions.hint: Look at the first letter of each term. How many letters are skipped between neighbouring terms?

steps.explain: Write the first letters.
steps.work: Acid → A, Electron → E, Joule → J, Pressure → P.

steps.explain: Count how many letters of the alphabet are skipped each time.
steps.work:
A [bcd] E: 3 skipped.

E [fghi] J: 4 skipped.

J [klmno] P: 5 skipped.

So the next gap skips 6 letters.

steps.explain: P is the 16th letter. Move on 7 places (skip 6, land on the 7th).
steps.work: P [qrstuv] W: the next letter is W. 16 + 7 = 23, the 23rd letter.
